links.note: 782 says friendship with the wise fills like the crescent moon while that of fools shrinks like the moon after full (மதிப் பின்னீர பேதையார் நட்பு). 811 says of the characterless (பண்பிலார்), even when they seem to drink one in, that shrinking is sweeter than growing (பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது). What 782 states as the natural course of a bad friendship, 811 turns into something to be welcomed.

783 says the bond with people of character (பண்புடையாளர் தொடர்பு) gives more the more it is practised (பயில்தொறும்), like a book re-read. 811 takes the opposite case, பண்பிலார் கேண்மை, and says its growth is worse than its decline. Together they show that 783's rule of friendship improving with use holds only where பண்பு is present.

In 1266 the waiting wife says that when her husband returns she will drink him in (பருகுவன்) so that her pain ends. 811 uses the same verb for friends who look as though they would drink one up (பருகுவார் போலினும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as from excess of love. The pair shows 'drinking' as the book's figure for consuming affection, sincere in the wife's mouth and only an appearance in the bad friend.

839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting from them brings no pain (பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில்). 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses (பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்) the friendship of those who befriend when there is profit and leave when there is none. Both measure a worthless friendship by the same test: its loss costs nothing.

812 treats the friendship of those who leave when the gain ends (அறின் ஒரூஉம்) as a matter of indifference, gained or lost. 799 says that the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when recalled at the hour of death (உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). Read together, losing such a friend is no loss, yet having trusted one is not painless.

Both verses name the ஒப்பிலார். 812 says it makes no difference whether their friendship is had or lost; 800 goes further and says to leave it even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). Parimelazhagar explains the word differently in each place: here as those who fit with no one because they look only to their own gain, there as those who do not accord with the world.

813 sets friends who weigh what will come to them (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) beside 'those who take what they get' (பெறுவது கொள்வார்), whom Parimelazhagar identifies as courtesans, and thieves. 912 describes those women directly: they weigh the profit and then speak of character (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The later chapter spells out the comparison 813 makes in a phrase, with the same verb தூக்கு for the calculating look.

103 praises help done by those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி) as greater than the sea. 813 ranks friendship that does weigh its return (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும்) with courtesans and thieves. The two verses hold the same view from opposite sides: whether a person weighs the gain is what separates the best help from the worst friendship.

798 says not to take the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு). 814 uses the same compound, ஆற்றறுக்கும், for the untrained horse (கல்லாமா) that fails its rider on the battlefield, and concludes that solitude is better than such people as one's own. 814 supplies the image for 798's plain instruction, and raises it from 'do not take' to 'better alone'.

788 defines friendship by the moment of need: like the hand of a man whose garment slips, it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது). 814 pictures the reverse, a horse that gives way in the battle itself (அமரகத்து). Both locate the test of a friend at the instant of crisis, one by the hand that acts unasked and one by the mount that fails.

781 asks what guard is as hard for hostile action to get past as friendship (வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு). 815 says the poor friendship of the small does not become a protection even when made (செய்தேமஞ் சாரா, in Parimelazhagar's reading) and is better not had. 815 limits 781: friendship is a guard only when the friend is not one of the சிறியவர்.

106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு). 815 says the friendship of the small, which gives no safety (ஏமம்), is better not obtained at all. The same measure, support in trouble, decides in one verse which friends must be kept and in the other which should never be acquired.

797 says that gain for a person is giving up the friendship of fools (பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). 816 says that ஏதின்மை with the wise, which the index reads as being a stranger and Parimelazhagar and Pope as enmity, is ten million times better than close intimacy with a fool (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு). 816 gives the scale for 797's claim: even the worst relation to the wise is preferred to the best with a fool.

450, on a king's counsellors, says that letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse (பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்தே) than taking on the enmity of many. 816 says a fool's close friendship is worth less by a crore than the wise man's ஏதின்மை. Both rank relationships by arithmetic and both put the quality of one's companions above the number or friendliness of them.

784 says friendship is not for laughing (நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல்) but for rebuking when one oversteps. 817 says that what comes from enemies is a hundred million times better than friendship of the laughing kind (நகைவகையராகிய நட்பு), which Parimelazhagar explains as friends like jesters who amuse, take their profit and go. 817 applies 784's definition as a verdict: a friendship that is only laughter is worth less than enmity.

639 says seventy crore enemies are better (எழுபது கோடி உறும்) than a minister at one's side who plots harm. 817 says enemies are ten crore times better (பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்) than friends who are all laughter. The same construction and the same judgment appear in court and in friendship: an open enemy is preferred to someone close who is of no real use or worse.

789 says friendship sits enthroned where one supports the other without wavering in every way one can (ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை). 818 describes those who make difficulties over a task that is within their power (ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்றுபவர்) and says to let that friendship slip without a word. The shared verb ஒல்லு ties them: the friend 818 drops is the one who fails 789's standard although able to meet it.

800 says to leave the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார் even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). 818 says to let a friendship with those who hold back what they could do lapse without speaking of it (சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்). Both are about how to end a friendship, not whether: one accepts a cost, the other avoids an open break.

664 says that speaking is easy for anyone and acting as one has spoken is hard (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). 819 says the bond with those whose deed is one thing and word another (வினைவேறு சொல்வேறு பட்டார்) is bitter even in a dream. 664 treats the gap between word and deed as a common weakness; 819 shows that in a friend it is not excused.

799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin burns the heart even to think of at the time of death (அடுங்காலை உள்ளினும்). 819 says the bond with those whose words and deeds differ is painful even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). Each verse extends the harm of a false friend beyond ordinary waking life, to the deathbed in one and to sleep in the other.

182, in the chapter on backbiting, says that destroying a person behind their back and smiling falsely to their face (புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை) is worse than denying virtue. 820 says to keep away entirely from those who are intimate at home and defame one in the assembly (மனைக்கெழீஇ மன்றில் பழிப்பார்). The same two-faced conduct is judged first as a wrong in the one who does it and then as a danger to be avoided in choosing friends.

188 asks what people whose habit is to broadcast even the faults of those close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers. 820 warns against the bond with those who are friendly in private and blame one in public. Both take the public exposure of an intimate as the mark of a person no one should be near.

883 says to fear the enemy within, because at the moment of weakness (உலைவிடத்து) it cuts like the tool that cuts the potter's clay (மட்பகை). 821 says the friendship of those who join without inner accord (நேரா நிரந்தவர்) is an anvil (பட்டடை) for striking once they find the right opening (சீரிடம் காணின்). Both verses use a craftsman's tool for the hidden enemy and both place the blow at the moment that suits him.

487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but watch for the time and burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). 821 warns that those who keep close without inner consent will strike when they see the right place. The patience the book recommends to a ruler in 487 is the same conduct it tells him to expect from a false friend in 821.

882 says not to fear enemies who are like swords but to fear the bond with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 822 says the friendship of those who seem one's own and are not (இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார்) will turn. Both identify the enemy in the guise of kin as the dangerous one; 882 gives the instruction and 822 the reason, that such a bond does not stay what it looks like.

822 uses women's minds as its example of something that changes (மகளிர் மனம்போல வேறுபடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this of women in general and supports it with a line from the Valaiyapathi. 974 takes single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) as its model of the constancy that greatness needs. On Parimelazhagar's general reading of 822 the two figures conflict; if 822's மகளிர் is limited to the courtesans of chapter 92, they do not.

920 lists two-minded women (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்) with liquor and dice as the company of those fortune has left. 822 compares false friendship to women's minds that become other (வேறுபடும்). The divided or shifting female mind serves in both as the book's figure for a tie that cannot be relied on, and 920 suggests which women the figure has in view.

373 says that however many subtle books one studies (நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும்), one's own inborn understanding prevails. 823 says that even after learning many good things (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும்) it is hard for the மாணார், whom Parimelazhagar takes as enemies, to become good in mind. The same limit on learning is stated for fate and for enmity: study does not override what a person already is.

834 says no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught others and still does not restrain himself (தானடங்கா). 823 says much good learning rarely makes the unworthy good at heart (மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் அரிது). Both deny that learning by itself changes character; Parimelazhagar draws the practical point for 823, that one should not count a person a friend on account of his learning.

786 says that befriending so that the face smiles is not friendship; befriending so that the heart within smiles is (முகநக ... அகநக). 824 describes those who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா) and says they are to be feared. 786 only denies such people the name of friend; 824 names them deceivers (வஞ்சர்) and makes them a danger.

706 says that as crystal shows what is next to it, the face shows what is strongest in the heart (நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்). 824 says there are deceivers whose faces smile sweetly while they are hostile inside. If 706 is read as a general fact about faces the two conflict; if it holds only for a trained reader of signs, as its chapter suggests, 824 describes what the untrained observer sees.

93 places virtue in a glad face, a kind look and sweet words that come from within (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து ... அகத்தானாம் இன்சொல்). 824 shows the face and the inside (முகம், அகம்) separated: a sweet smile over a bitter heart. The pair shows why 93 adds அகத்தானாம்: the outward half of its description can be had without the inward one.

509 says to trust no one without examining them and, having examined, to trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 825 says that those who are not at one with you in mind are not to be judged trustworthy by their words in any matter (சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று). 825 adds to the rule of examination a statement of what cannot count as evidence.

890 says that life with those who are not in accord (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) is like living with a snake in a hut. 825 says those whose minds are not settled with yours (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are not to be trusted on their words. Both make inner agreement, not outward closeness or speech, the thing that decides whether a person near you is safe.

1096, spoken by the lover, says that though they speak like strangers, the words of those who bear no anger are quickly understood (செறாஅர்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்). 826 says that though they speak good things like friends, the words of enemies are quickly understood (ஒட்டார்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்). The two verses share a frame and closing phrase and are mirror images: speech fails to hide the feeling behind it, whether love or enmity.

709 says the eye itself tells of enmity and friendship (பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know how to read it. 826 says an enemy's words are soon recognised even when they sound like a friend's. Both hold that hostility shows through the surface; 709 makes this depend on a skilled reader, a condition 826 leaves unstated.

826 says the words of the unreconciled are quickly seen through although they say good things as friends do. 828, in the same chapter, says a weapon can lie hidden in hands joined in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்) and in an enemy's tears. 828 limits the confidence of 826: the speech may give itself away, but gestures of submission and grief can still conceal the intent.

488 advises that on meeting an enemy one should bear him, which Parimelazhagar glosses as bowing, until his end is in sight (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை). 827 says not to accept an enemy's bowing speech (சொல்வணக்கம்), because the bending of a bow signals harm. The humility 488 teaches as a tactic is the humility 827 teaches one to distrust in the other side.

279 says the arrow is straight and cruel while the lute is bent and good, so people should be taken by what their actions produce (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). 827 says the bow's bend (வில்வணக்கம்) means harm, and so does an enemy's bending speech. Both draw on things that are bent to say that form does not show intent; 827 adds that who is bending decides what the bend means.

985 says that bowing (பணிதல்) is the strength of those who accomplish and the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 827 says that an enemy's verbal bowing should not be accepted, since it points to harm as a bent bow does. Bowing is a means of working on an adversary in both; 985 praises it in the worthy, and 827 says that from an enemy it must not be taken as goodwill.

555 asks whether the tears wept by those who suffer and cannot bear it (அழுதகண்ணீர்) are not the weapon (படை) that wears away a ruler's wealth. 828 says a weapon (படை) hides in an enemy's joined hands and that the tears he weeps (அழுதகண்ணீர்) are the same. The words tears and weapon are paired in both verses: in 555 real tears are themselves the weapon, in 828 feigned tears cover one.

71 says love cannot be bolted in, because the small tears of those who love make it public (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்). 828 says an enemy's tears can hide a weapon as his worshipping hands can. Tears reveal the heart in 71 and conceal it in 828, so the evidence 71 relies on is good only once it is known that the one weeping is ஆர்வலர் and not ஒன்னார்.

824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while bitter within. 829 says that those who make much of you outwardly and despise you (மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளுவார்) should be made to smile and be embraced within the friendship so that it dies (நகச்செய்து நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லல்). The response 829 prescribes has the same form as the conduct 824 warns against; Parimelazhagar notes that it is allowed as royal policy although such doubleness is otherwise unfitting.

488 says to bear an enemy when you meet him until his final limit comes, and then his head goes down. 829 says to keep the false friend pleased and hold him in the appearance of friendship while it dies inwardly. Both advise outward accommodation of an enemy who cannot yet be opposed openly, in the chapter on timing and in the chapter on false friendship.

786 says friendship of the smiling face is not friendship and only that of the smiling heart is (முகநக ... அகநக). 830 says that when the time comes that enemies act as friends, one should befriend with the face and drop friendship within (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). 830 uses 786's own pair of face and inside to prescribe, for this one case, the very thing 786 says is not friendship.

874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who treats enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 830 says that when an enemy becomes a friend (பகைநட்பாம் காலம்) the friendship should be shown on the face only, given up inwardly, and, in Parimelazhagar's reading, later dropped altogether. If 874 means a real turning of enemies into friends, as Pope renders it, the two disagree about whether such a friendship should be accepted in the heart; if 874 too means outward conduct only, they agree.

488 advises bearing with enemies when one meets them until their end is in view. 830 advises a friendly face toward enemies at a time when, as Parimelazhagar explains, they cannot be openly put aside. Both treat outward civility toward an enemy as a matter of timing and not of feeling.
